lead: A keyframe is a value the animator fixes at one chosen frame. A raised arm at frame 0 and the same arm down at frame 12 are two keys, and every frame between them is computed. That computation is tweening, also called interpolation or in-betweening, and it works the same way for position, scale, rotation, opacity or colour. Instead of drawing every frame, the animator draws the poses that matter and states the timing; the software fills the gaps. Every 2D timeline tool, CSS transition and game-engine animation clip is built on this one idea.
prereq: You need Chapter 5.1 for why keys are spaced unevenly: the gaps between them carry the sense of weight and speed.

sections.h3: Keys fix values; tweens fill the frames

blocks.text: A keyframe is a frame at which a property's value is stored explicitly. An in-between is a frame whose value is computed from the keys on either side. A tween is the whole run of in-betweens joining two keys, plus the rule used to compute them. Animators say in-betweening; some syllabi say interpolation animation. All three words describe the same machinery.

Each property is a separate channel with its own keys. Position x, position y, scale, rotation angle, opacity and each colour component carry independent key lists, so an object can slide fast while it fades slowly. A channel is a function: give it a frame number f and it returns a value v. The animation is that function, sampled once per frame.
The simplest rule is linear interpolation. The normalised time u runs from 0 at the first key to 1 at the second, and the value moves in step with it.
u = (f − f₁)/(f₂ − f₁),   v = v₁ + u(v₂ − v₁)
blocks.where: f is the frame being drawn; f₁ and f₂ are the key frames bounding it, with f₁ ≤ f < f₂; v₁ and v₂ are the property values at those keys, in the same unit (px, degrees, or 0 to 1 for opacity); u is normalised time; v is the value at frame f.

blocks.text: Hand-editing an in-between rarely sticks, because the next redraw recomputes it. To change the motion, move a key, add a key, or change the interpolation rule. Keys do not need to be dense; a two-key tween across 30 frames is normal.

Linear motion starts and stops at full speed, which reads as mechanical. Easing reshapes u before it is used: the value is still the start value plus progress times the value gap, but progress is no longer u itself.
s(u) = u²  (ease-in);   s(u) = 1 − (1 − u)²  (ease-out);   s(u) = u²(3 − 2u)  (ease-in-out)
blocks.where: u is normalised time from 0 to 1 and s(u) is the eased progress, also 0 to 1. Ease-in starts slow and speeds up, ease-out does the reverse, ease-in-out does both. The value is v₁ + s(u)(v₂ − v₁). These three polynomials are the usual textbook choices; every tool ships a family of similar curves.

blocks.text: Easing changes speed, never the path. At the halfway time of an ease-in, s(0.5) = 0.25, so the object has covered only a quarter of the distance and looks like it is gathering momentum. That is slow-in slow-out from Chapter 5.1, written as arithmetic.

Spline interpolation goes one step further: each key also stores a tangent, the rate at which the value is changing as it passes. A cubic Bezier in (frame, value) space links two keys with continuous slope, so velocity has no kink at the key. The same Bezier maths as vector paths in Chapter 5.8 applies, with time on one axis instead of paper.

The graph editor is where this becomes visible: frames along the bottom, values up the side, keys as points, handles as tangent stalks. Flatten a handle and the object decelerates into that key; pull it steep and the object shoots through. Reading that curve tells you the motion without playing it back.

sections.h3: Shortest rotation, and duration counted in frames

blocks.text: Angles wrap at 360°, so plain subtraction lies. From 350° to 10° the raw difference is 10 − 350 = −340°, which spins the object most of a turn backwards. The short way is +20°. Wrap the difference into the range (−180°, 180°].

blocks.where: v₁ and v₂ are the start and end angles in degrees; mod is the non-negative remainder; d is the signed shortest turn in degrees, between −180° and +180°; u is normalised time; s is the easing function. Add the interpolated turn to the start angle and wrap the result into 0°–360° for display.

blocks.text: Tools let the animator override the wrap: typing 710° instead of 350° as the end angle forces a full extra turn forward, which is what a spinning wheel or a coin flip needs. The number you store is the number that is interpolated.

Duration is a frame gap, not a key count. A ten-frame tween is ten frames at any frame rate, but the seconds change: 10 ÷ 24 = 0.417 s at 24 fps and 10 ÷ 30 = 0.333 s at 30 fps. Speed in px/s is Δvalue × fps ÷ Δframes. Exporting at a frame rate different from the timeline's silently changes how fast everything moves.

Two families get separate names. A motion tween interpolates properties of one object. A shape tween interpolates one outline into another and needs the two outlines matched point by point first — Chapter 5.3. Timeline panels, tween paths and motion blur belong to Chapter 5.9.

spec.aria: A graph of x in pixels against frame from 0 to 10: a straight line from the key at 20 px to the key at 120 px with a dot at every frame, and dashed guides marking 75 px at frame 5.5.

examples.question: A logo slides across a banner. A keyframe at frame 0 holds x = 20 px; the next keyframe at frame 10 holds x = 120 px. The tween is linear and the project runs at 24 fps. Find x at frames 2, 4, 6 and 8, and the time at which x = 75 px.
steps: Frame gap: Δf = 10 − 0 = 10 frames. Value gap: Δx = 120 − 20 = 100 px.
Linear step per frame = 100 px ÷ 10 frames = 10 px per frame, constant.
Frame 2: x = 20 + 10 × 2 = 40 px. Frame 4: 60 px. Frame 6: 80 px. Frame 8: 100 px.
For x = 75 px, normalised time u = (75 − 20) ÷ 100 = 0.55.
Frame = 0 + 0.55 × 10 = 5.5. A renderer shows a whole frame, so it would output frame 5 (x = 70 px) or frame 6 (x = 80 px).
Time at 24 fps: t = 5.5 ÷ 24 = 0.2292 s, about 229 ms after the first key.
examples.answer: x = 40, 60, 80 and 100 px at frames 2, 4, 6 and 8; x = 75 px at frame 5.5, which is 0.2292 s after the start at 24 fps.
examples.check:
x1, x2, f1, f2 = 20.0, 120.0, 0, 10
step = (x2 - x1) / (f2 - f1)
for f in (2, 4, 6, 8):
    print(int(x1 + step * (f - f1)))
u = (75 - x1) / (x2 - x1)
frame = f1 + u * (f2 - f1)
print(frame)
print(round(frame / 24, 4))

traps: Tweening rotation the long way round: 350° to 10° is +20°, not −340°.
Treating the number of keyframes as the duration. Duration is the frame gap between two keys, not how many keys you placed.
Editing an in-between by hand and expecting it to stay — it is recomputed on the next redraw.
Mixing frames and seconds. A 10-frame tween is 0.417 s at 24 fps and 0.333 s at 30 fps, so px/s depends on the frame rate.
Assuming easing bends the path. It only changes how fast the value travels along the same path.

quiz.q: Define keyframe, in-between and tween in one line each.
quiz.a: A keyframe stores a property value at a chosen frame; an in-between is a frame whose value is computed from neighbouring keys; a tween is the whole run between two keys plus the interpolation rule.

quiz.q: Why does an ease-in tween suit a hand reaching for a cup better than a linear one?
quiz.a: A real hand starts from rest and accelerates. Ease-in covers little distance early (s(0.5) = 0.25) and more later, so the value curve matches that acceleration. Linear motion jumps to full speed at once and reads as mechanical.

quiz.q: What does the graph editor plot, and what does the slope of the curve mean?
quiz.a: Frame number across, property value up, keys as points with tangent handles. The slope at any point is the property's rate of change, that is its speed.

quiz.q: A key at frame 0 holds y = 300 px and a key at frame 20 holds y = 100 px, linear. Find y at frame 5 and the frame at which y = 150 px.
quiz.a: Δy = 100 − 300 = −200 px over 20 frames, so −10 px per frame. Frame 5: y = 300 − 50 = 250 px. y = 150 px needs a drop of 150 px, which is 15 frames, so y = 150 px at frame 15.

quiz.q: An object rotates from 350° at frame 0 to 10° at frame 12, linear, taking the shortest path. Give the angle at frames 3, 6 and 9.
A 12-frame tween looks right in a 24 fps preview but too fast in a 30 fps export. Explain what changed and give both durations.
quiz.a: The frame gap stayed 12; only the frame rate changed. 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 s and 12 ÷ 30 = 0.4 s. Each frame is held for less time, so the motion finishes sooner and top speed in px/s rises by 30 ÷ 24 = 1.25 times.

quiz.q: Why does a spline tween need tangent handles when a linear tween does not?
quiz.a: A linear tween fixes one constant velocity inside each segment and lets velocity jump at the key. A spline sets both the value and the slope at each key so velocity is continuous across keys; the handle is how the animator states that slope.

beyond: Not for the exam. CSS exposes this machinery as transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(a, b, c, d), and Lottie files carry keyframe arrays straight from an authoring tool into phone apps. In 3D the shortest-arc idea generalises to quaternion slerp, and modern game engines often blend several clips or search a motion database instead of interpolating two poses. Search next: cubic-bezier easing, quaternion slerp, Lottie keyframe JSON.
